headline: A Midjourney Engineer Ends the Web's 30-Year Text Layout Bottleneck
lede: Every time a browser needs to know how tall a block of text is, it freezes, recalculates the position of every element on the page, and then answers. That single architectural constraint has quietly limited web design for three decades. Pretext, a 15-kilobyte JavaScript library released on March 27, 2026 by Cheng Lou, a senior engineer at Midjourney, bypasses it entirely — measuring text through the browser's Canvas engine instead of its layout tree.
body:
The premise behind every website you have ever used is a layout engine conceived in the mid-1990s for static documents. When a browser renders a paragraph, it shapes glyphs, measures widths, determines line breaks, and positions each line — a pipeline that finishes invisibly for a blog post, but becomes catastrophically expensive the moment a developer needs to know how much space text will occupy *before* rendering it. That act of asking triggers a **forced synchronous reflow**: the browser pauses script execution, flushes every pending style change, and recalculates its entire *layout tree*. For a single measurement, the cost is tolerable. For five hundred — as in a chat application rendering message bubbles, or an AI interface streaming tokens line by line — it produces *layout thrashing*: hundreds of full recalculations per frame, each potentially consuming 20 to 30 milliseconds when the entire budget for smooth animation is 16.6.

Pretext proposes a structural alternative. Rather than querying the browser's layout engine for text dimensions, it uses the Canvas API — specifically the `canvas.measureText()` method — which taps the same underlying font-shaping engine but operates entirely outside the layout tree and triggers no reflow. A `prepare()` call segments the text using the browser's `Intl.Segmenter` API (handling Unicode, right-to-left scripts, CJK per-character breaks, and emoji sequences) and caches the measured width of each segment. After that, a `layout()` call — the *hot path* invoked on every resize, scroll, or streaming update — is pure arithmetic: it adds segment widths until a line overflows, then begins the next. The library has no dependencies.

Lou comes to the problem with unusual credentials. Before joining Midjourney (the AI image-generation company), he was a member of the React core team at Meta (META) and creator of `react-motion`, a physics-based animation library with more than 21,000 GitHub stars. He co-created ReasonML, the typed functional language that later became ReScript. His prior work was always concerned with a similar question: how to make dynamic, time-varying UI state legible to the browser without paying unnecessary rendering costs. He built Pretext over roughly a month using an AI-assisted iteration loop — running Claude and Codex against large multilingual corpora, including public-domain texts in Thai, Chinese, Korean, and Arabic — to reconcile the library's arithmetic against actual browser output.

The performance claims require some qualification. Lou's benchmarks, corroborated by writeups on InfoQ and Hacker News, compare the hot path of `layout()` — operating on pre-cached measurements — against a loop of raw DOM reads. The result is roughly 0.05 milliseconds versus 30 milliseconds: a 600-fold difference. Lou himself acknowledged the comparison is not symmetric: it pits a cached computation against an uncached DOM query. A fairer test — batched DOM reads against a warmed Pretext cache — is less dramatic, but for real-time applications like AI token streaming or drag-to-resize editorial layouts, still consequential. The library's demo page, which renders passages from Leopold Aschenbrenner's *Situational Awareness* flowing dynamically around draggable orbs at 120 frames per second, illustrates scenarios that are not achievable with DOM-based measurement.

The reason CSS, the web's official styling language, never solved this is instructive. The CSS Shapes specification, finalized in 2014, introduced a `shape-outside` property that lets text wrap around non-rectangular floated elements — the typographic trick long used in print. But `shape-outside` depends on the browser float mechanism, which confines text to one side of an object at a time. The inverse, `shape-inside` — letting text fill an arbitrary shape — was specified in CSS Shapes Level 2 and never implemented in any shipping browser. Dynamic shapes, updated as a user drags a panel or a new token arrives, require a DOM write followed by a DOM read, returning directly to the reflow problem. Eleven years after the spec was finalized, web developers still had no native answer. Pretext collected more than 16,000 GitHub stars in its first 24 hours.

concepts.definition: When JavaScript reads a geometric property from the DOM — element height, width, scroll position — the browser must first flush all pending style changes and recompute the layout of the entire page before it can return the value. This mandatory pause is called a forced synchronous reflow. It can take 10–100 milliseconds on a complex page and blocks all other work on the main thread while it runs.

The performance pathology that occurs when JavaScript alternates between writing to the DOM and reading geometric measurements from it in a loop. Each read forces a full reflow; each write invalidates the layout tree, requiring the next read to trigger another full recalculation. A loop measuring 500 element heights triggers 500 full layout passes. Chrome DevTools flags this pattern with red entries in the performance timeline.

The browser's internal data structure recording the computed position, size, and geometry of every element on the page. It is built from the DOM and the CSS cascade. Any change to a property that affects an element's size or position invalidates part or all of the tree, requiring it to be recomputed before any geometric measurement can be read back.

A browser API providing a 2D drawing surface that operates entirely outside the DOM layout system. Because it does not participate in the layout tree, calling its methods — including `measureText()`, which returns the pixel dimensions of a string in a given font — does not trigger reflow. Pretext exploits this to perform text measurement cheaply.

A CSS specification, finalized in 2014, that allows text to wrap around non-rectangular floated elements via the `shape-outside` property. It covers circles, ellipses, polygons, and alpha-masked images. The inverse capability — `shape-inside`, letting text flow within an arbitrary container shape — was specified in Level 2 of the standard and never implemented by any shipping browser.

In performance engineering, the section of code that executes most frequently per unit of time — the innermost loop of an animation, a resize handler, or a streaming render. Optimizing the hot path is the primary lever for frame-rate improvement because even small savings compound across hundreds of calls per second.

A browser API that divides a string into grapheme clusters, words, or sentences according to Unicode rules and locale-specific conventions. Unlike splitting on spaces, it correctly handles Chinese and Japanese text (no spaces between words), Arabic ligatures, and emoji sequences composed of multiple code points joined by zero-width joiners.

books.title: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead
books.author: Leopold Aschenbrenner
books.summary: A self-published long-form essay released in 2024 by Leopold Aschenbrenner, a former OpenAI researcher, arguing that artificial general intelligence will likely arrive within a few years and that the United States is already in a quiet national-security race to develop it before China. It circulated widely in AI research and policy circles as a frank insider account of the pace of capability development. Its text appears as demo content in Pretext's official demo page, flowing dynamically around draggable orbs as a showcase for the library's editorial layout engine.

repos.summary: Pretext is a 15KB, zero-dependency TypeScript library for measuring and laying out text in the browser without touching the DOM layout tree. It uses a two-phase approach: a `prepare()` call that caches segment measurements via Canvas, and a `layout()` call that performs pure arithmetic to determine line breaks and block height at 120fps. The library supports Unicode, RTL scripts, CJK, emoji ZWJ sequences, and soft hyphens, and integrates with any JavaScript framework.

fact_check: The tweet claims Pretext is “500x faster.” Lou's own benchmarks and independent writeups cite a range of roughly 300–600x, with the comparison specifically pitting Pretext's cached hot path against an uncached loop of DOM reads — the most pathological possible baseline. Lou himself described the comparison as “unfair” while defending that the hot path is what matters for real-time streaming UIs. The “500x” figure falls within the stated range but describes the ceiling rather than the typical case, and omits the caching caveat. The tweet's claim that editorial text layout has been “basically impossible” for 30 years is rhetorical: CSS Shapes and JavaScript workarounds exist, but they are expensive, fragile, or too limited for dynamic use cases. The underlying diagnosis is accurate even if the framing is sharper than the evidence strictly supports.
